'''Superstatistics'''<ref name=beck>{{cite journal|last1=Beck|first1=C.|last2=Cohen|first2=E.G.D.|title=Superstatistics|journal=[[Physica A]]|volume=322|pages=267–275|year=2003|doi=10.1016/S0378-4371(03)00019-0|arxiv = cond-mat/0205097 |bibcode = 2003PhyA..322..267B }}</ref><ref name=cohen>{{cite journal|last1=Cohen|first1=E.G.D.|title=Superstatistics|journal=[[Physica D]]|volume=139|number=1|pages=35–52|year=2004|doi=10.1016/j.physd.2004.01.007|bibcode = 2004PhyD..193...35C }}</ref> is a branch of [[statistical mechanics]] or [[statistical physics]] devoted to the study of [[non-linear]] and non-[[Stability theory|equilibrium]] [[system]]s. It is characterized by using the [[Superposition principle|superposition]] of multiple differing [[statistical model]]s to achieve the desired non-linearity. In terms of ordinary statistical ideas, this is equivalent to compounding the distributions of random variables and it may be considered a simple case of a [[doubly stochastic model]].

Consider<ref name=hanel>{{cite journal|last1=Hanel|first1=R.|last2=Thurner|first2=S.|last3=Gell-Mann|first3=M.|author-link3=Murray Gell-Mann|title=Generalized entropies and the transformation group of superstatistics|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]| volume=108|issue=16|year=2011|pages=6390–6394|  pmc=3080995| doi=10.1073/pnas.1103539108|arxiv = 1103.0580 |bibcode = 2011PNAS..108.6390H |s2cid=8931463|doi-access=free}}</ref> an extended [[thermodynamical system]] which is locally in [[Thermodynamic equilibrium|equilibrium]] and has a [[Boltzmann distribution]], that is the probability of finding the system in a state with energy <math>E</math> is proportional to <math>\exp(-\beta E)</math>. Here <math>\beta</math> is the local inverse temperature. A non-equilibrium thermodynamical system is modeled by considering macroscopic fluctuations of the local inverse temperature. These fluctuations happen on time scales which are much larger than the microscopic relaxation times to the Boltzmann distribution. If the fluctuations of <math>\beta</math> are characterized by a distribution <math>f(\beta)</math>, the ''superstatistical Boltzmann factor'' of the system is given by

:<math>
B(E)=\int_0^\infty d\beta f(\beta)\exp(-\beta E).
</math>

This defines the superstatistical partition function
:<math>
Z = \sum_{i=1}^W B(E_i)
</math>
for system that can assume discrete energy states <math>\{E_i\}_{i=1}^W</math>. The probability of finding the system in state <math>E_i</math> is then given by

:<math>
p_i=\frac{1}{Z}B(E_i).
</math>

Modeling the fluctuations of <math>\beta</math> leads to a description in terms of statistics of Boltzmann statistics, or "superstatistics". For example, if <math>\beta</math> follows a Gamma distribution, the resulting superstatistics corresponds to Tsallis statistics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://tsallis.cat.cbpf.br/biblio.htm|title = CBPF - Grupo de Física Estatística/Group of Statistical Physics}}</ref> Superstatistics can also lead to other statistics such as power-law distributions or stretched exponentials.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Beck|first=Christian|title=Stretched exponentials|journal=Physica A|year=2005|volume=365|pages=96–101|doi=10.1016/j.physa.2006.01.030|arxiv=cond-mat/0510841|s2cid=2972692}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ourabah|first1=K|last2=Gougam|first2=L A|last3=Tribeche|first3=M|title=Nonthermal and suprathermal distributions as a consequence of superstatistics|journal=Physical Review E|volume=91|issue=1|article-number=012133|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.91.012133|pmid=25679596|year=2015|bibcode=2015PhRvE..91a2133O}}</ref> One needs to note here that the word super here is short for superposition of the statistics.

This branch is highly related to the [[exponential family]] and [[Mixing (mathematics)|Mixing]]. These concepts are used in many approximation approaches, like particle filtering (where the distribution is approximated by delta functions) for example.
